study.title: Judges 20 - The war against Benjamin and the tragedy of Gibeah
study.overview: This chapter narrates Israel's reaction to the terrible crime committed in Gibeah, the city of Benjamin. The assembly of the whole nation seeks to discern what to do, requires justice from the Benjaminites, and ends up entering into a devastating civil war. The text highlights both Israel's moral zeal against wickedness and the gravity of sin when justice is refused and violence multiplies. In the end, although the cause against evil is legitimate, the outcome reveals almost the total ruin of a tribe of Israel and the sadness of a nation without just government.

outline.title: National Assembly and Decision against Gibeá
outline.explanation: Israel meets as one people before the LORD in Mizpah to ascertain the crime against the concubine of the Levite. The report is publicly presented, and the House decides that it will not return to its tents until it deals with the shame of Gibeah. There is military organization and intention to take the case as a national judgment against the abomination committed.

outline.title: Benjamin's refusal and the first failures of Israel
outline.explanation: The tribes ask Benjamin to deliver the guilty, but the tribe protects the men of Gibeah and prepares for war. Israel consults the LORD and receives direction, but suffers two heavy defeats. After weeping, fasting, offering sacrifices and consulting again, he receives the promise of victory the next day.

outline.title: Victory by ambush and almost extermination of Benjamin
outline.explanation: Israel uses an ambush strategy: it pretends to retreat, attracts the Benjaminites, fires Gibeah and the fences with great destruction. The LORD delivers Benjamin into the hands of Israel, but the battle ends with great death. Only six hundred men flee to the Rimmon's cliff, while the rest of the tribe and their cities suffer severe judgment.

study.context: The chapter takes place at a time when Israel had not yet king, and this helps to explain the moral and political disorder of the text. The meeting in Mispah acts as a national assembly before the LORD, and the presence of Fineias no v. 28 suggests, according to the notes provided, that the facts occurred shortly after the death of Joshua. The historical setting is not used to exalt Israel, but to show the contrast between the holy vocation of the people and their inability to maintain justice wisely.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that public sin cannot be treated with indifference: Israel acts correctly by demanding justice against Gibeah's wickedness. However, it also shows that a just cause can be conducted in a disorderly way, with excess confidence, precipitation and great suffering. There is tension here between justice and mercy: Benjamin aggravates guilt in protecting the guilty, but Israel's reaction almost exterminates an entire tribe. Theologically, the text denounces the decomposition of the life of covenant when there is a lack of just leadership and when the people fail to seek the Lord with humble dependence. Israel's initial defeats show that not always the numerical superiority or justness of the cause guarantee success; obedience, reverence and discernment are needed. The practical expression of this appears in crying, fasting, sacrifices and successive consultations, indicating that the people only advance when they recognize their limitation before God.

scholarViews.insight: Matthew Henry points out that the meeting in Mispah was spontaneous and marked by holy zeal for the honor of God and Israel, not by a common chief.

Adam Clarke notes that the expression "before the Lord" can indicate consultation and prayer in the name of God, and not necessarily only the physical location of Shiloh; he understands Mispah as a place of assembly before God.

questions: When indignation against sin is just, how can it prevent it from turning into hardness, revenge or excess?
What do Israel's initial defeats teach about relying only on strength, number or cause itself?
In what situations does the protection of a collective sin end up making the whole community a part of guilt?
study.practice: The chapter calls the reader to take sin seriously, but also to treat justice with fear of God and self-control. In practice, this means not covering up evil, not romanticizing violence and not assuming that being right enough to act correctly. In real conflicts, the biblical response includes discernment, sincere pursuit of God, repentance, prayer, humility and willingness to correct one's own way before seeking victory over the other.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not allow to state with certainty the exact location of Mispah in this episode or the precise chronological relationship with other events, although Adam Clarke suggested closeness to Joshua's days because of Fineias. There is also an ancient textual variation in some numbers of deaths mentioned by Clarke, but the general sense of the chapter does not depend on this difference. It is not possible to conclude more than the text and notes actually say about the detailed historical identity of the places and dates.
